    The Citi AAdvantage Globe Card awards 5,000 Loyalty Points for every four qualifying American Airlines flight segments, up to three times per status qualification year.

    Industry observers note that these are segments, so a roundtrip with a connection each way is four flights. Three of those trips can generate the full bonus. Six nonstop roundtrips would do it, too.

    Industry observers note that you don’t have to buy the tickets with your Globe card. You can use another card for its rewards or protections, or fly on a ticket your employer purchases, and still earn the bonus on your qualifying travel.

    Industry observers note that these are points toward status, not another 15,000 miles you can spend on awards. For someone already flying American regularly, this can reduce how much additional spending or other earning they need to do to reach their next status level. There’s no requirement to divert $20,000 or $50,000 of purchases from a more rewarding card. I view the card as an inexpensive way to purchase Loyalty Points which are valuable both for earning status and for additional milestone rewards.

    When I analyzed Globe at launch, my criticism was that Citi wasn’t giving customers much reason to keep spending on it. From the customer’s perspective, though, that’s potentially a good thing. I earn the flight bonus while putting spend wherever it makes the most sense. The Executive card by contrast includes 10,000 bonus Loyalty Points at each of 50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000 Loyalty Points earned in a qualification year. Globe’s Flight Streak bonus can stack with that. Someone meeting all the requirements can earn up to 55,000 bonus Loyalty Points from the two products combined. The final Executive bonus requires reaching 240,000 Loyalty Points, so that maximum isn’t a shortcut to earning Executive Platinum from scratch. My second Citi AAdvantage Globe Card came from the April 2026 Barclays conversion. I initially wondered whether two accounts would generate two sets of flight bonuses. American subsequently confirmed to me that they wouldn’t. The Initial Bonus And Annual Fee The current offer for the Citi AAdvantage Globe Card is 60,000 AAdvantage miles after $4,000 in purchases within the first three months. The annual fee is $350, isn’t waived the first year, and there’s no additional charge for authorized users. There are no foreign transaction fees. The bonus restriction is specific to the Citi AAdvantage Globe Card: you can’t have received a upcoming account bonus on Globe within the past 48 months, and there’s also a restriction involving another Citi account with a recent bonus that you converted into Globe. Simply having the Executive or Business card doesn’t disqualify you. What You Earn When You Spend The card’s earning categories are: Eligible Purchases AAdvantage Miles Per Dollar Loyalty Points Per Dollar AAdvantage Hotels bookings 6 1 American Airlines purchases 3 1 Restaurants, including takeout and delivery 2 1 Eligible transit, including taxis, rideshares and public transit 2 1 Other purchases 1 1 Bonus categories increase redeemable miles, not Loyalty Points. A $500 eligible American Airlines purchase earns 1,500 miles and 500 Loyalty Points from the card, in addition to whatever the passenger earns for flying. The 6 miles per dollar on eligible AAdvantage Hotels bookings are separate from the miles and Loyalty Points awarded for the hotel reservation itself. (Reserve Now, Pay Later bookings don’t qualify for the card’s 6-mile earning rate.) For my own spending, Executive already offers 4 miles per dollar on eligible American purchases (and at 4 points per dollar, I actually prefer my Chase Sapphire Reserve® [See rates and fees]) and 12 on eligible AAdvantage Hotels bookings. Globe’s Splurge Credit can give me a reason to charge a particular hotel purchase to it, but the regular earning rate doesn’t. For everyday purchases, one American mile and one Loyalty Point per dollar can make sense when you’re trying to reach a status threshold. Otherwise, there are better returns available. Holding Globe doesn’t obligate you to make it your everyday spending card. It’s a good card to have, not a daily spend driver outside of the quest for status. Four Admirals Club Passes Each Calendar Year Globe comes with four digital Admirals Club passes each calendar year. Each is valid for 24 hours after activation, including visits to multiple Admirals Clubs during that period. The access rules make these especially useful for an occasional traveler with children: Each adult needs a pass. Each adult using a pass can bring up to three children under 18. The primary cardmember must be present, including when using passes for adult companions. You need a same-day eligible American Airlines or oneworld boarding pass. Unused passes expire at the end of the calendar year. A couple traveling with two young children would use two passes for a travel day, rather than four. But you can’t give the passes to relatives traveling without you, and these aren’t Flagship Lounge passes or a full membership with partner lounge privileges. In my experience, the usual capacity restrictions on purchased one-day passes don’t apply to Globe passes. And just because you see a sign saying day passes aren’t being accepted doesn’t mean they aren’t being accepted – sometimes they just don’t take away the sign. American sells ordinary day passes for $79. That doesn’t make four Globe passes worth $316 to everyone. I already have Admirals Club membership through Executive, so I don’t assign these passes additional value for my own access. The Companion Certificate Doesn’t Require Annual Spending After renewing the card, starting in your second cardmembership year, you receive a certificate for one companion to travel on an eligible domestic roundtrip for $99 plus taxes and fees when you buy a qualifying Main Cabin roundtrip. However, this isn’t a certificate for any flight you want. It has fare inventory restrictions and restricted dates. You book through American Airlines Meeting Services, and travel generally must be within the contiguous 48 states on American or American Eagle. Residents of Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands have exceptions allowing qualifying trips from home to the lower 48. It doesn’t cover basic economy or partner flights. The primary cardmember must travel. The account must remain open for a full billing cycle after the anniversary month, and Citi allows 8–10 weeks for the certificate to become available. The certificate is valid for 12 months from issuance, with booking and travel completed by its expiration. I’ve gotten good savings from Barclays companion certificates, so I don’t dismiss these. If the eligible companion ticket would otherwise cost $500, replacing that with $99 plus taxes can cover much of the annual fee. The Credits Are Worth What They Save You Citi advertises more than $750 in value. I wouldn’t start with that number, but several benefits overlap with what I already have, and others require purchases I wouldn’t otherwise make. Up to $100 annual Splurge Credit. Choose up to two eligible merchants at a time from AAdvantage Hotels, 1stDibs, Future Personal Training and Live Nation. Activate your selection at Citi’s Splurge Credit page before purchasing. This is $100 total (not $100 per merchant). Eligible AAdvantage Hotels bookings are likely the most practical use for many readers. Up to $100 in annual inflight credits. Use the card for eligible purchases on domestic American Airlines or American Eagle flights. Food, drinks and eligible Wi-Fi purchases can qualify. This is less valuable when drinks are already included in your seat or status benefits, or when your flight has free Wi-Fi. Up to $240 annually with Turo. This is up to $30 per completed trip, so it takes eight trips to get the full amount. Link the card at Turo’s Globe page and pay with it directly; digital wallet payments don’t qualify. I wouldn’t assign this much value unless I were already using Turo regularly. Up to $120 for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck every four years. Useful if you need it, but I have plenty of other cards offering this reimbursement. My original reaction to the Splurge Credit was that it wasn’t worth much to me. I already have plenty of hotel credits. And an AAdvantage Hotels booking generally means giving up the hotel points, elite night credit and status benefits you’d receive by booking directly with a chain. I like the inflight credit myself now that American offers more food for purchase on more flights – I get one item free as an Executive Platinum member but I can buy sandwiches and snacks for my family. The calendar-year benefits also improve the first year. Open a card in November, and you can use available credits and passes before year-end and receive fresh allotments in January, before the next annual fee. Flight Streak resets in March. The companion certificate starts after renewal. Bags, Boarding And Other Benefits Of The Citi AAdvantage Globe Card The card provides a first checked bag free on qualifying domestic American Airlines itineraries for the primary cardmember and up to eight companions on the same reservation. Group 5 boarding also covers up to eight companions. You don’t have to pay for the tickets with Globe. Those can be valuable for someone without status, particularly a family traveling together. They add little for me because my existing status already provides better benefits. Your AAdvantage miles also don’t expire while you’re the primary holder of an eligible AAdvantage credit card. There’s also a 10% discount on eligible non-flight components of American Airlines Vacations packages booked through the designated Citi booking page. The travel and purchase protections include trip cancellation and interruption, trip delay, lost or damaged luggage, rental car coverage, extended warranty and purchase protection. Rental coverage is secondary in your country of residence. Citi Entertainment and Mastercard’s World Legend benefits add access to selected ticketing, dining and other experiences. I’ll Pay $350 To Keep The Citi AAdvantage Globe Card If you only want a checked bag and earlier boarding, Citi® / AAdvantage® Platinum Select® World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees] is cheaper. If you want regular Admirals Club access, Executive provides a membership for its $695 annual fee. Globe earns its place with the combination of flight bonuses, occasional lounge access and a companion certificate without an annual spending requirement. There’s a case for holding Globe alongside Executive for the additional Loyalty Points. Here’s how I’d look at renewal. If you get a real $100 of savings from the Splurge Credit, there’s $250 of annual fee left to justify through the flight bonus, companion certificate and other benefits. Earning all 15,000 Flight Streak Loyalty Points at that cost works out to about 1.67 cents per point before assigning any value to the remaining benefits. An extra 15,000 that gets you to the next status level is much more useful than points that leave you between thresholds. For someone flying at least 12 qualifying segments and pursuing American status, I think Globe is a strong addition even with another AAdvantage card.     Industry News: Mamdani’s ‘Affordability’ Deception

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • New Yorkers are coming to terms with the unenviable conditions they’ve voted themselves into, with some experiencing sticker shock and a commensurate degree of buyer’s remorse.
    • Sources indicate that new York Times reporter Emma Fitzsimmons could not have anticipated the garment-rending apoplexy that her social media post would inspire in city officials.
    • Noah Rothman is a senior writer at National Review.

    New Yorkers are coming to terms with the unenviable conditions they’ve voted themselves into, with some experiencing sticker shock and a commensurate degree of buyer’s remorse. Who could blame them? The response from Democrats to the public’s frustrations should only further reinforce the unavoidable conclusion that New Yorkers have populated city government with neophytes and ignoramuses.

    Sources indicate that new York Times reporter Emma Fitzsimmons could not have anticipated the garment-rending apoplexy that her social media post would inspire in city officials. Nevertheless, she fulfilled her reportorial duties when, after completing her Amazon.com purchase of a children’s liquid vitamin, she encountered this message from the online retailer: “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order,” it read. “Act now to protect low prices.”.

    Noah Rothman is a senior writer at National Review. His third book, Blood and Progress: A Century of Left-Wing Violence, was published by Hachette in May 2026.

    On “Mamdani’s ‘Affordability’ Deception”.

    #76814. Hyatt Keeps Pepsi For 10 More Years At 700+ U.S. Hotels—Even Though Few Guests Want It

    Hyatt Keeps Pepsi For 10 More Years At 700+ U.S. Hotels—Even Though Few Guests Want It

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4243 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Hyatt has signed up for another 10 years with Pepsi, covering more than 700 U.S.
    • According to recent reports, no, it isn’t.
    • The renewal announced November 19, flagged by The Bulkhead Seat, doesn’t cover every Hyatt brand or every country.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Hyatt has signed up for another 10 years with Pepsi, covering more than 700 U.S. hotels. After Marriott finally decided to switch to Coca-Cola, Hyatt is sticking with the beverage that prompts a question nobody wants to hear: Is Pepsi okay? No, it isn’t. I rarely drink soda. When I do, I don’t want to waste it on Pepsi. The renewal unveiled November 19, flagged by The Bulkhead Seat, doesn’t cover every Hyatt brand or every country. But the economics of choosing Pepsi make more sense once you realize that the person negotiating the contract isn’t the one that has to drink it. Which Hyatt Brands Are Covered, And Where Can You Get Coke? The agreement covers U.S. hotels in Hyatt’s Classics and Essentials portfolios. Translating Hyatt’s brand groupings: Portfolio Brands Classics Grand Hyatt, Hyatt Regency, Destination by Hyatt, Hyatt Centric, Hyatt Vacation Club, Hyatt Essentials Hyatt Place, Hyatt House, Hyatt Studios, Hyatt Select, Caption by Hyatt, Unscripted by Hyatt UrCove also belongs to Essentials, but its Chinese hotels aren’t covered by a U.S. agreement. The Luxury, Lifestyle and Inclusive Collection portfolios aren’t part of this deal. No one wants to show up at an Andaz or Park Hyatt and get told they can’t have a Coke. Alila, Thompson, The Standard, and Hyatt Ziva and Zilara are also outside the deal’s scope. Here are some hotels that have specifically listed Coke: Hotel Coca-Cola On The Menu Park Hyatt New York Room service lists Coke and Diet Coke Andaz Maui Meeting and event menus list Coke and Diet Coke Thompson Dallas Room service lists Coke and Diet Coke Alila Marea Beach Resort Encinitas Room service lists bottled Coke Pepsi Doesn’t Have To Be Your First Choice To Win The Business When I covered Marriott’s switch in April, Marriott told hotels that more than 70% of its guests favored the Coca-Cola portfolio. Hotels choose suppliers based on the total deal: product pricing, rebates, equipment, servicing, marketing support and sometimes direct payments. We can see how this works in a public contract. Fresno, California’s 2018 Pepsi agreement for its convention center offered a $20,000 annual sponsorship payment, a 25% vending commission, $3 rebates per case or gallon sold, bulk pricing and equipment maintenance in exchange for exclusive beverage rights. A hotel has a modestly captive audience. You’ve already booked the room, your conference is downstairs, or you’re sitting by the pool. You can buy a Coke elsewhere, but that takes effort. Some people accept Pepsi. Others choose something else. The hotel loses some beverage sales and creates some disappointment. But it still thinks it can come out ahead if its supplier prices and rebates are better and they aren’t seeing guests change their hotel bookings. In other words, the worse product can be more profitable to the hotel – or at least to Hyatt corporate. Here, Hyatt brings access to guests whose hotel decision usually turns on something other than soda. Pepsi doesn’t have to persuade all those guests that it tastes better (it doesn’t). Getting its products stocked on property can shift purchases without changing anyone’s preferences. PepsiCo also brings Gatorade, Starbucks ready-to-drink coffee, Quaker, Lay’s, Doritos, Muscle Milk and poppi. “Is Pepsi Okay?” Was Never A Compliment The question assumes you’ve requested something else and asks whether you’ll accept a substitute you didn’t want. Pepsi understood the problem well enough to build its 2019 Super Bowl commercial around it, recruiting Steve Carell, Cardi B and Lil Jon to insist Pepsi was “More Than OK.” John Belushi’s Olympia Restaurant on Saturday Night Live had already reduced the experience to “No Coke! Pepsi!” You could order what you wanted. You were getting what the restaurant had decided to sell. The Pepsi Challenge, New Coke, And What A Recipe Can’t Copy I remember the Pepsi Challenge as a kid. I remember how scared Coke seemed, and the debacle of New Coke. The explanation popularized by Malcolm Gladwell in Blink is that Pepsi’s sweetness does better in a sip test than when someone drinks a whole can. Maybe some people really did prefer the first sip of Pepsi and then found the rest too much. That never seemed right to me. The first sip of Coke is much better. Fortunately, there’s no rule you have to finish a soda. Coca-Cola’s history of New Coke says the organization’s lead over its chief competitor had been slipping for 15 consecutive years. It introduced the reformulated drink on April 23, 1985, after taste tests involving nearly 200,000 consumers favored the new formula. The original came back just 79 days later. The tests hadn’t captured how people would react to having their Coke taken away.     Appeals court stands by LaMonica McIver ruling

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., is seen on Capitol Hill last December.
    • LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., faced a setback Thursday in her effort to ditch charges tied to a scuffle during an oversight visit at an immigration detention facility last year, as a federal appeals court declined to reconsider its decision to let the case move forward.
    • In a recent development, the decision by the U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., is seen on Capitol Hill last December. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Industry observers note that rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., faced a setback Thursday in her effort to ditch charges tied to a scuffle during an oversight visit at an immigration detention facility last year, as a federal appeals court declined to reconsider its decision to let the case move forward.

    In a recent development, the decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit leaves in place a 2-1 opinion from August which held that McIver was not immune from the charges, which stemmed from a confrontation between visiting members of Congress and federal agents while at the Delaney Hall facility in Newark. McIver has challenged the charges, arguing that her visit fell under the “speech or debate” immunity she has as a member of Congress because she was there to inspect detention conditions.

    In a statement McIver mentioned she and her attorneys were looking at “every possible option” in response to the appeals court ruling. Her statement invoked the Trump administration’s threats to treat oversight efforts as criminal conduct and said “we are all one step closer to a world in which the president of the United States can try to imprison people simply because he does not like what they stand for.”.

    “Donald Trump continues to send warning shots to Democrats in Congress and in all levels of power — but their case against me right now, in broad daylight, goes well beyond a warning. Because of a weaponized Department of Justice and because I dared to do my job and conduct oversight of ICE, I am facing 17 years in prison,” McIver mentioned in her statement.

    Following Thursday’s decision on rehearing, McIver could next ask the Supreme Court to weigh in on the case.

    The August majority opinion from Judge Cindy Chung, which Thursday’s decision leaves in place, said that two of the three charges against McIver did not fall under the immunity, which is limited to legislative acts. The majority sent the third charge back to the lower court for another ruling.

    “We have considered the ‘nature’ of the charged conduct and concluded it is unambiguously non-legislative,” the judge wrote.

    Separately, Judge Thomas Ambro partially dissented to offer a different approach to the case. Ambro would have required the trial judge to more closely examine the exact conduct McIver was charged with, as well as to examine whether the Trump administration targeted her because of her political views.

    “I would allow her discovery into the truth of the matter — not only for her own sake but to safeguard the independence of our legislative bodies,” Ambro wrote.

    Ambro did not vote on whether the full 3rd Circuit should rehear the case. Three judges voted to have the full 3rd Circuit hear McIver’s case, and Judge Emil Bove, a former Trump administration official and former personal attorney for the president, did not participate in the vote.

    In a recent development, the criminal case started shortly after the Delaney Hall visit in May 2025, as prosecutors alleged that McIver assaulted federal agents during a scuffle around Newark Mayor Ras Baraka. Officials arrested Baraka that day and charged him with trespassing, but later dropped those charges.

    Court filings in the case alleged that McIver struck agents during the confrontation. McIver has argued that she was effectively being charged for doing her job and federal agents were interfering with her attempts to inspect the facility.

    It has been revealed that earlier this year, Judge Jamel K. Semper of the U.S. District Court for the District of Upcoming Jersey disagreed and ruled that the case could move forward.

  • Holiday travel often brings higher costs, crowded airports and unpredictable delays, but certain card benefits can help mitigate these challenges.
  • Key perks include free checked bags, expedited security screening, lounge access, ride-hailing and food-delivery credits, and hotel privileges like early check-in or complimentary breakfast.
  • Many travel cards offer statement credits for airport security programs and ride services, as well as elite status with hotels or rental car companies to streamline your journey.
  • Selecting the right card depends on your travel habits and which benefits will save you the most money or time during peak travel periods.
  • Some benefits, such as free checked bags or lounge access, may require enrollment or payment with a specific card and can have restrictions on eligible companions or locations.
  • Application and enrollment for airport security programs should be completed well in advance, as processing times can be lengthy.
  • Hotel and rental car elite status benefits often require linking loyalty accounts and confirming eligibility before travel.

December 3, 2025: Another passenger the gesture after a trip with delays and seating problems. They said they hadn’t even contacted United about the previous trip. January 5, 2026: A passenger said a solo flight three weeks earlier had been delayed two hours. On the subsequent trip, both the passenger and their fiancée received Economy Plus. Jon’s example adds a customer without status, which is especially useful – United may not be using a ‘customer value score’ and limiting whom they’re reaching. And the January example suggests a companion can benefit even when they weren’t on the disrupted flight. Recipients generally appreciated being remembered. The Silver member in the August thread liked the gesture even though they expected to get Economy Plus at check-in anyway. Economy Plus is extra legroom coach. This upgrade isn’t to first class or long haul business. American Had Eagle Scores Years Ago Back in 2018, I wrote about the long-standing American Airlines Helix system and customer Eagle ratings. Those scores combined how valuable a customer was with how badly American had treated them and their risk of leaving. The one-to-five rating was recalculated daily. A high spending customer whose flights went smoothly didn’t necessarily receive the highest score. Neither did someone with terrible experiences who brought little revenue. The system helped employees decide when to make exceptions and spend more to preserve a customer relationship. One practical consequence was that customers with sufficiently high Eagle ratings could get expiring systemwide upgrades extended. Other airlines have remembered past problems, too. British Airways’ 2012 Know Me announcement described telling crew about a regular customer’s earlier weather delay so they could acknowledge it and thank the passenger for returning. Delta’s 2017 onboard recognition tool included recent flight interruptions among the reasons to flag someone for attention. British Airways and Delta were recognizing the earlier problem. United is pairing that with a better seat. United Has Been Talking About Recovery At the Barclays investor conference in February, chief financial officer Mike Leskinen discussed using technology for getting displaced crews and disrupted customers where they needed to go. And United’s Sheryl Lee described presenting Flight Finder at this year’s Grounded in Iceland conference. That tool looks for open seats for disrupted passengers already on standby. This also fits Scott Kirby’s public argument for technology that anticipates customer needs, and a pattern I’ve covered at United: making customer milestones visible to employees and offering selected travelers Global Services treatment they weren’t expecting. Airlines collect enormous amounts of customer information. The hard and useful part is actually doing something with it. But Here The Next Booking Has Already Happened The economics of this can be very good. If an Economy Plus seat would otherwise go unsold, giving it to an inconvenienced passenger costs United very little. The passenger gets something the airline normally charges for, and the message tells them why. Waiting until close to departure gives them more information about which seats they’re likely to sell. But an unannounced benefit delivered after booking can’t persuade someone to make that booking in the first place. A credit or an advance offer of a better seat can give an angry customer a reason to try the airline again. This gesture reaches people who already have another United reservation. And that doesn’t mean they’ve forgiven the airline. Their next trip could have been purchased before the bad trip. United may have the only convenient nonstop. They may be flying because their employer booked it. I especially like, though, that this can reach someone without status. An empty extra legroom seat may do more to win that customer’s business than offering the same thing to a frequent flyer who already gets it regularly. And United has to get the seat choice right. I wouldn’t consider moving from an aisle to a middle seat an improvement just because it’s in Economy Plus, and by the way United doesn’t offer free drinks in their extra legroom coach seats like even American does.     #76805. Lame-Duck Senators Should Not Be Able to Block Good Judicial Nominees

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (210 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nationalreview ↗ Open Full Page

    Lame-Duck Senators Should Not Be Able to Block Good Judicial Nominees

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (210 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, senator John Cornyn recently blocked the nomination of the eminently qualified T.
    • In a recent development, the “blue slip” privilege does not exist in the Constitution or even in the Senate Rules.
    • Dave Yost is senior counsel and vice president of policy innovation at Alliance Defending Freedom.

    In a recent development, senator John Cornyn recently blocked the nomination of the eminently qualified T. Elliot Gaiser to the federal district court in Texas, preferring a favorite-son candidate whom President Trump did not nominate. But the Constitution is clear: The nomination belongs to the president, not the distinguished senator. The constitutional power to “advise and consent” does not belong to a single senator, but to the Senate as a whole. Senator Cornyn’s use of a long-standing privilege conveyed by his colleagues usurps the power of both the president and the Senate.

    In a recent development, the “blue slip” privilege does not exist in the Constitution or even in the Senate Rules. It is a practice of the Judiciary Committee not to advance a judicial nominee to a vote without the approval of both of the State’s senators. Invented in 1916, its scope and application are entirely within the discretion of the Senate Judiciary chairman, Chuck Grassley. He ought to use his discretion to put Gaiser’s nomination to a vote.

    Dave Yost is senior counsel and vice president of policy innovation at Alliance Defending Freedom. He previously served as the attorney general of Ohio.

    On “Lame-Duck Senators Should Not Be Able to Block Good Judicial Nominees”.

    #76804. Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (939 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (939 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Collins took sole responsibility for a larger share of Maine earmarks.
    • After a bruising reelection defeat, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, is ready to play hardball.
    • Eager to show how much she's delivered for her constituents, Collins took the lion's share of credit in her committee's fiscal 2027 spending bills for Maine earmarks — at the expense of her delegation colleague, independent Angus King, who caucuses with Democrats.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Collins took sole responsibility for a larger share of Maine earmarks. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    After a bruising reelection defeat, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, is ready to play hardball.

    Eager to show how much she's delivered for her constituents, Collins took the lion's share of credit in her committee's fiscal 2027 spending bills for Maine earmarks — at the expense of her delegation colleague, independent Angus King, who caucuses with Democrats.

    The amount of earmarks King secured fell dramatically compared to his previous year's total in Senate Appropriations Committee bills, as Collins took sole credit for most earmarks both senators had requested.

    The power play has instigated a dispute over how to award credit for "congressionally directed spending," better known as earmarks. It has also raised questions about a Senate rule that requires committee leaders to disclose the name of each senator who requested projects to be included in a spending bill before it can move on the floor.

    Recent findings suggest that it’s undeniable that as the chair of the spending panel, Collins has more influence over which projects reach the final bills than her delegation mate. Collins spokesperson Phoebe Keller stated that since available earmark funding is split into separate pots for the majority and minority to dole out, the bills reflect which of those funding sources was tapped to provide money to the relevant projects.

    Keller said that Collins deserves sole credit for the contested projects, as listed in the reports accompanying the bills.

    "When only Collins is listed, it reflects only she chose to fund the project,” Keller said.

    A Democratic committee aide contested that characterization, saying that traditionally all requesters are named regardless of which party’s funding allocation is tapped for a project.

    “The handling of these particular projects is a clear departure from the norm and will need to be rectified in conference negotiations,” the aide remarked.

    King is credited with approximately $54 million in fiscal 2027 earmarks in the bills Collins released this month, including joint projects with Collins. That's down from around $231 million in the Senate's fiscal 2026 bills, according to a CQ Roll Call analysis.

    Recent findings suggest that last year, King and Collins were both listed on 75 of the 77 projects that both requested that were included in the Senate bills, with just two carrying only Collins’ name. This year, Collins claimed sole responsibility for over $125 million in projects that both she and King requested, approximately two-thirds of the joint requests.

    While King’s overall requests fell by more than $200 million this year versus last, his success in securing requested funds plummeted at a far greater rate with less credit for overlapping projects.

    The joint requests for which Collins claimed sole credit include five for the Maine Department of Transportation in the Transportation-HUD bill, including $10.7 million for northern freight rail improvements; $9.6 million for Route 26 reconstruction in Oxford; and $7.2 million for improvements in Rockport, among others.

    In the Labor-HHS-Education bill, projects Collins took sole credit for include $4 million for the University of Maine for biology laboratory equipment and just over $4 million for the creation of a modern emergency helipad at Lincoln Hospital.

    And the Interior-Environment bill features $4 million each for wastewater improvements in Limestone and Kennebec that both Collins and King asked for but are only attributed to Collins, among others.

    Similarly, the Agriculture, Commerce-Justice-Science and Homeland Security bills all include a project requested by both senators that only Collins is listed as securing in the bill.

    The outgoing Appropriations chair’s ability to fuel billions of dollars in federal funding for her state during her career was the centerpiece of her ultimately unsuccessful campaign for reelection, which she lost to Democrat Troy Jackson.

    As written, the draft bills appear to risk running afoul of a Senate rule that requires the committee’s chair to identify each senator who requested projects in a bill online at least 48 hours before a vote to advance the legislation on the floor.

    The relevant rule, Senate Rule 44, states that it is out of order to vote on a motion to proceed to consider a bill unless the chairman of the committee certifies that “each congressionally directed spending item . . . has been identified through lists, charts, or other similar means including the name of each Senator who submitted a request to the committee for each item so identified.”.

    That information must be “available on a publicly accessible congressional website in a searchable format at least 48 hours before such vote.”.

    A King spokesman called on the spending panel to add his name to the relevant requests.

    “We believe this must have been an oversight and assume the committee will upgrade the requests —per Senate rules — once it’s called to their attention,” King spokesman Matthew Felling said.

    In a recent development, the bills released by Collins are drafts, and no floor action on final fiscal 2027 spending bills is expected this Congress. There’s limited time left before the Dec. 11 spending deadline, when all current funding is set to expire, and Democrats want to wait to negotiate final bills until they retake majorities in both chambers next year.

    But to comply with the rule, before the bills reach the floor the reports accompanying the bills, that includes the earmark tables, may have to be rewritten to list King on the contested projects, or the committee may need to disclose the information elsewhere online.

    Both chambers unveiled stricter ethics guidelines surrounding earmarks in 2021 when the practice returned after a decade-long ban.

    Peter Cohn contributed to this report.

    #76803. Delta’s CEO Says It Flew To LaGuardia In The 1950s—It Didn’t, But His Predecessors Figured Out How To Win Upcoming York

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 44m • 📚 Deep Dive (8750 w)

    Business & Policy 📈 Bullish 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    Delta’s CEO Says It Flew To LaGuardia In The 1950s—It Didn’t, But His Predecessors Figured Out How To Win Upcoming York

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 44 min read (8750 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~44 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, delta CEO Ed Bastian says flying from Atlanta to LaGuardia takes longer today than when Delta released the route in the 1950s.
    • Delta’s Fresh York service began at Newark.
    • Today it takes more time to fly from Atlanta to LaGuardia than it did in the 1950s when we first launched that flight, which is absurd.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, delta CEO Ed Bastian says flying from Atlanta to LaGuardia takes longer today than when Delta released the route in the 1950s. Except Delta didn’t fly to LaGuardia in the 1950s. Delta’s Latest York service began at Newark. It took another 13 years to start LaGuardia. And the distinction between serving New York and serving the airport a New Yorker actually wants has been costing airlines money ever since. Speaking with Fortune, Bastian stated: Today it takes more time to fly from Atlanta to LaGuardia than it did in the 1950s when we first launched that flight, which is absurd. Delta’s history gives its LaGuardia launch date as October 1, 1969. Northeast and Northwest Airlines, which Delta later absorbed, served LaGuardia in 1945. But there was no Delta Atlanta–LaGuardia service in the 1950s. The airline that became such a powerful force in New York was a late arrival, built through acquisitions, deals with competitors, and an understanding of what New Yorkers would put in their wallets. The Mayor Who Refused To Get Off His Plane In New Jersey On November 24, 1934, New York Mayor Fiorello La Guardia arrived from Chicago on TWA. The plane landed at Newark. The mayor refused to get off. His ticket said New York. This was New Jersey. After an argument, the aircraft took him onward to Floyd Bennett Field in Brooklyn. He told the New York Times, “my ticket says New York and that’s where they brought me.” He repeated the stunt the following month. He wasn’t demanding to be taken to what’s now New York LaGuardia. That airport wouldn’t open until 1939. He was promoting New York City’s existing airport in Brooklyn, trying to pull airline business across the state line. Ironically, Floyd Bennett Field was about the same distance from Times Square as Newark. Delta’s First New York Flights Landed At Newark Delta didn’t grow up as a New York airline. Its roots were in Southern crop dusting, and its headquarters moved to Atlanta in 1941. Eastern had a substantial head start in the New York–Atlanta market. Back then an airline couldn’t just decide to add a route. The federal government’s Civil Aeronautics Board decided who could fly where. Delta’s 1956 annual report says its new route award allowed three daily round trips between New York and Newark. The launch timetable reveals flight 724 leaving Atlanta at 6:05 p.m. and arriving at Newark at 9:21 p.m., with a Washington stop. That’s 3 hours 16 minutes. Comparing that one-stop propeller service with today’s nonstop wouldn’t tell us much about air traffic control in any case… Delta was already selling New York from Manhattan ticket offices, including Rockefeller Plaza. It added Idlewild, today’s JFK, on May 15, 1957. The airline’s August 1957 timetable shows Delta’s four-engine Flying Scot daytime coach flights using Idlewild, while its other flights used Newark. Why Did LaGuardia Take Until 1969? Delta had arrived late in a regulated market, and LaGuardia was difficult to get into. Eastern and American each essentially had a concourse to themselves, while the other airlines shared the remaining two. Delta initially served the airport with relatively small DC-9s, while Eastern already had 727s. Delta began advertising LaGuardia in its August 1969 timetable, Flight 620 will begin operating upon completion of arrangements for terminal facilities at LaGuardia. The actual October 1969 launch schedule offered non-stop service, not available from Delta’s 1950s service. Flight Leaves Atlanta Arrives LaGuardia Scheduled time 168 6:15 a.m. 8:15 a.m. 2 hours 620 12:10 p.m. 2:08 p.m. 1 hour 58 minutes 622 6:15 p.m. 8:13 p.m. 1 hour 58 minutes The 1956 annual report advertised a future Atlanta–New York time of 1 hour 41 minutes aboard forthcoming DC-8 jets, which Delta hadn’t introduced yet. How Delta Bought Its Way Into Being A New York Airline A Civil Aeronautics Board examiner recommended giving Delta New York–Miami authority in 1956, but the board itself rejected that awarding the service to Northeast. Sixteen years later, Delta bought Northeast. That 1972 acquisition brought a much stronger position in New York, Boston and Florida. In 1991, Delta acquired Pan Am’s transatlantic operation and its Northeast shuttle. Then came the deal that changed the scale of LaGuardia. Proposed in 2009 and completed in 2011, the US Airways slot swap gave Delta 132 daily LaGuardia slot pairs. US Airways received 42 daily Washington National pairs, $66.5 million, and rights for additional São Paulo service. The Government Accountability Office measured Delta’s LaGuardia slot share rising from 24% in April 2011 to 44% in May 2012. Regulators required slots to go to smaller competitors as a condition of approval. At LaGuardia, JetBlue received eight daily pairs and WestJet another eight. JetBlue actually bid the most for both packages, but the auction rules wouldn’t let one airline win both. Then, as I reported in 2024, following Enilria’s examination of slot trades, Delta even managed to get back the eight round trips WestJet had received as a competition remedy. Slots handed to a rival to keep Delta’s expansion competitive wound up back with Delta. US Airways helped Delta grow at LaGuardia. United would help at JFK. When United pulled out in 2015, Delta took over its JFK slots under a long-term lease. Delta also spent money leveraging that access with its $4 billion LaGuardia terminal project. United Tried To Prove Newark Was New York Using Taxi Ads Newark is a New York metropolitan airport. Depending on where you’re going and the traffic, it can be the most convenient one. It also serves a large and wealthy New Jersey market in its own right. United’s digital taxi top campaign showed real-time driving estimates to Newark and JFK. The advertising industry’s account reveals the best detail: when Newark wasn’t the quickest, the display switched to generic United branding. The comparison disappeared when United lost it. When United left JFK in 2015, that meant premium Los Angeles and San Francisco service to Newark. After Scott Kirby joined United, he called the decision a mistake. The airline had looked at the money its JFK flights made or lost. Kirby explained that leaving also helped American win corporate accounts such as Disney and Time Warner. Those customers bought travel beyond Los Angeles–New York, including Los Angeles–London. United returned to JFK in 2021, then left again in 2022 after failing to obtain the access it wanted to build a larger operation. Its Blue Sky partnership with JetBlue provides another way back: access for up to seven daily United round trips from JFK’s new Terminal 6 as early as 2027, alongside reciprocal loyalty benefits and the ability to sell each other’s flights. Winning New York Also Means Winning Credit Card Spending I’ve made the same argument about American’s retreat in major markets. An airline needs to be useful where high-spending customers live. Otherwise why would those customers choose its credit card? A New Yorker who wants LaGuardia for domestic trips and JFK for longer journeys is a candidate for a Delta Amex (even though those miles are worth less than competing currencies). Delta’s investor presentation connects large coastal metropolitan economies with its premium and loyalty growth. In 2023 Delta described its cobrand spending as approaching 1% of U.S. GDP. Using American Express’s disclosures for that year—Delta represented about 10% of $1.680 trillion in worldwide network volume—implies roughly $168 billion. Against the contemporary $27.36 trillion estimate of U.S. GDP, that’s about 0.61%. As I’ve argued, they’re rounding generously. And there’s a bigger problem with the growth story. When Delta renewed its American Express deal in 2019, it projected $7 billion annually by 2023. It delivered $6.8 billion. That sounds like nearly hitting the target, until you account for how much pandemic-era inflation had shrunk the value of each dollar – in a way that hadn’t been anticipated in 2019. Consumer prices rose about 19% between 2019 and 2023. Using annual consumer price indexes, the $6.8 billion payment had only about $5.7 billion of 2019 purchasing power. Delta nearly hit its 2019 goals in nominal terms due to inflation, but its actual performance was a real miss. Delta now expects more than $9 billion from American Express in 2026. It’s an enormous business, but it’s had a ceiling greater than what Delta had hoped in 2019 – which also explains the importance of free wifi, Uber and Starbucks – looking for new customers anywhere they can find them. The poor return on spending of a Delta credit card finally matters. Ultimately, though, Delta wasn’t born a New York airline. Ed Bastian’s predecessors assembled one, including airport access its competitors willingly gave up. United is still working to repair its decision to leave JFK. For customers who insist that their New York ticket take them to a particular New York airport, being told Newark is close enough still doesn’t close the sale. And Bastian’s 1950s comparison is typical Bastian – never let facts like connecting service and which airport the airline served get in the way of the story he wants to tell. Sixteen years later, Delta bought Northeast. That 1972 acquisition brought a much stronger position in New York, Boston and Florida. In 1991, Delta acquired Pan Am’s transatlantic operation and its Northeast shuttle. Then came the deal that changed the scale of LaGuardia. Proposed in 2009 and completed in 2011, the US Airways slot swap gave Delta 132 daily LaGuardia slot pairs. US Airways received 42 daily Washington National pairs, $66.5 million, and rights for additional São Paulo service. The Government Accountability Office measured Delta’s LaGuardia slot share rising from 24% in April 2011 to 44% in May 2012. Regulators required slots to go to smaller competitors as a condition of approval. At LaGuardia, JetBlue received eight daily pairs and WestJet another eight. JetBlue actually bid the most for both packages, but the auction rules wouldn’t let one airline win both. Then, as I reported in 2024, following Enilria’s examination of slot trades, Delta even managed to get back the eight round trips WestJet had received as a competition remedy. Slots handed to a rival to keep Delta’s expansion competitive wound up back with Delta. US Airways helped Delta grow at LaGuardia. United would help at JFK. When United pulled out in 2015, Delta took over its JFK slots under a long-term lease. Delta also spent money leveraging that access with its $4 billion LaGuardia terminal project. United Tried To Prove Newark Was New York Using Taxi Ads Newark is a New York metropolitan airport. Depending on where you’re going and the traffic, it can be the most convenient one. It also serves a large and wealthy New Jersey market in its own right. United’s digital taxi top campaign demonstrated real-time driving estimates to Newark and JFK. The advertising industry’s account reveals the best detail: when Newark wasn’t the quickest, the display switched to generic United branding. The comparison disappeared when United lost it. When United left JFK in 2015, that meant premium Los Angeles and San Francisco service to Newark. After Scott Kirby joined United, he called the decision a mistake. The airline had looked at the money its JFK flights made or lost. Kirby explained that leaving also helped American win corporate accounts such as Disney and Time Warner. Those customers bought travel beyond Los Angeles–New York, including Los Angeles–London. United returned to JFK in 2021, then left again in 2022 after failing to obtain the access it wanted to build a larger operation. Its Blue Sky partnership with JetBlue provides another way back: access for up to seven daily United round trips from JFK’s new Terminal 6 as early as 2027, alongside reciprocal loyalty benefits and the ability to sell each other’s flights. Winning New York Also Means Winning Credit Card Spending I’ve made the same argument about American’s retreat in major markets. An airline needs to be useful where high-spending customers live. Otherwise why would those customers choose its credit card? A New Yorker who wants LaGuardia for domestic trips and JFK for longer journeys is a candidate for a Delta Amex (even though those miles are worth less than competing currencies). Delta’s investor presentation connects large coastal metropolitan economies with its premium and loyalty growth. In 2023 Delta described its cobrand spending as approaching 1% of U.S. GDP. Using American Express’s disclosures for that year—Delta represented about 10% of $1.680 trillion in worldwide network volume—implies roughly $168 billion. Against the contemporary $27.36 trillion estimate of U.S. GDP, that’s about 0.61%. As I’ve argued, they’re rounding generously. And there’s a bigger problem with the growth story. When Delta renewed its American Express deal in 2019, it projected $7 billion annually by 2023. It delivered $6.8 billion. That sounds like nearly hitting the target, until you account for how much pandemic-era inflation had shrunk the value of each dollar – in a way that hadn’t been anticipated in 2019. Consumer prices rose about 19% between 2019 and 2023. Using annual consumer price indexes, the $6.8 billion payment had only about $5.7 billion of 2019 purchasing power. Delta nearly hit its 2019 goals in nominal terms due to inflation, but its actual performance was a real miss. Delta now expects more than $9 billion from American Express in 2026. It’s an enormous business, but it’s had a ceiling greater than what Delta had hoped in 2019 – which also explains the importance of free wifi, Uber and Starbucks – looking for new customers anywhere they can find them. The poor return on spending of a Delta credit card finally matters. Ultimately, though, Delta wasn’t born a New York airline. Ed Bastian’s predecessors assembled one, including airport access its competitors willingly gave up. United is still working to repair its decision to leave JFK. For customers who insist that their New York ticket take them to a particular New York airport, being told Newark is close enough still doesn’t close the sale. And Bastian’s 1950s comparison is typical Bastian – never let facts like connecting service and which airport the airline served get in the way of the story he wants to tell.     #76801. Rove Gives You 1,500 Free Miles Just For Signing Up—Plus 5,000 More On Your First $500 Hotel Booking

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    Rove Gives You 1,500 Free Miles Just For Signing Up—Plus 5,000 More On Your First $500 Hotel Booking

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1740 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Rove is offering 1,500 free miles just for signing up.
    • I’ve written quite a bit about Rove, and asked them to improve the offer available through my link.
    • They’ve also created a hotel booking code for readers:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Rove is offering 1,500 free miles just for signing up. You don’t have to book a trip, buy anything, or complete any other transaction. I specifically asked about an activity requirement, and Rove confirmed that new members get the miles instantly. I’ve written quite a bit about Rove, and asked them to improve the offer available through my link. This is three times the standard 500-mile referral signup bonus. Just like normal referrals, I receive Rove Miles when someone signs up through this link. It doesn’t cost you anything. In fact it gets you much more than not using this link. They’ve also created a hotel booking code for readers: 1,500 miles for joining: Use this link to create your new account. There’s no purchase requirement. 5,000 additional miles on your first hotel booking of $500 or more: Enter promo code VFTW when booking through Rove. A new member who uses both offers would earn 6,500 bonus miles, on top of the normal miles from their qualifying hotel booking. You can also just take the signup miles. And 5,000 miles on a $500 booking is twice what Rove offered at that spending level during its May promotion. What You Can Do With These Miles Rove is a free rewards program that lets you earn miles from hotel and flight bookings, online shopping, dining and gift cards. You don’t have to apply for a credit card, and you can earn rewards from the card you use to pay as well. Their transfer partners include familiar programs like Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France KLM Flying Blue, Qatar Airways Privilege Club and Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. They also have programs that are harder to access through the major bank currencies, including Lufthansa Miles & More (for better availability of business and first class awards), Japan Airlines Mileage Bank (better availability of awards, lower prices on partner awards), Air India Maharaja Club (United awards starting at just 3,500 points) and Copa ConnectMiles (Emirates awards with no fuel surcharges). Rove has a 2,000-mile minimum for partner transfers. You don’t need a hotel stay to earn additional miles. I’ve covered Rove’s dining program and instant gift card rewards, and just wrote about its personalized shopping offers of up to 25 miles per dollar. When The Hotel Bonus Makes Sense You can also redeem Rove Miles directly for travel. As I wrote last month, I can usually get around 1.5 cents apiece redeeming them for hotel stays that still earn hotel points and elite status credit. Using that benchmark, the 5,000-mile hotel bonus is worth about $75 toward travel. On a qualifying $500 booking, that’s an extra 15% in value before the booking’s regular rewards. Expressed another way, the promo adds 10 miles per dollar at exactly $500 in qualifying spend. I’ve been particularly interested in Rove’s Loyalty Eligible hotel rates. There are two different kinds of bookings to compare: Loyalty Eligible rates generally earn 5 Rove miles per dollar, while preserving eligibility for the hotel’s own points, elite night credit and status benefits. The hotel charges your card, which can make paying with that chain’s credit card attractive. Rove Rates can offer more Rove miles, with the site advertising up to 25 per dollar, but generally give up the hotel loyalty program earnings and benefits. That tradeoff is easier at an independent hotel where you wouldn’t earn chain points anyway. I’d take the free signup miles. For the hotel offer, enter VFTW and consider the rate you’re selecting before booking for the 5,000-mile bonus.     💡 Key Takeaways
    • As we get closer to final results from the 2026 midterms, the scale of the carnage comes more clearly into view.
    • It has been revealed that in the Senate, Democrats gained nine seats, the biggest swing since Republicans’ nine-seat pickup in 2014.
    • Dan McLaughlin is a senior writer at National Review Online and a fellow at National Review Institute.

    As we get closer to final results from the 2026 midterms, the scale of the carnage comes more clearly into view. The question is not whether Republicans can recover from this, but whether the American system of government will be changed irreparably before they do. To what will Republicans return?

    It has been revealed that in the Senate, Democrats gained nine seats, the biggest swing since Republicans’ nine-seat pickup in 2014. With 56 senators, it’s the Democrats’ biggest majority since 2009–10, when they peaked at 60 seats. Republicans haven’t had that many Senate seats since 1922, when the caucus was 59 seats after the 1920 landslide that repudiated Woodrow Wilson’s progressivism and swept Warren Harding into office. If you’re wondering, the largest-ever Republican Senate caucus, in absolute numbers rather than as a share of the chamber, was 60 in 1907; the largest Democratic caucus was 75 seats at the peak of the Upcoming Deal in 1937. There’s a reason why Franklin D. Roosevelt thought he could get away with Court-packing with 75 senators.

    Dan McLaughlin is a senior writer at National Review Online and a fellow at National Review Institute.

    On “The Real Stakes of the Wilderness Years”.

    #76796. House Democrats eye stock trading ban as early priority next Congress

    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    House Democrats eye stock trading ban as early priority next Congress

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1319 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, here at a news conference on Capitol Hill last week, says banning stock trading in Congress is a “high priority.” Now Democrats must decide what form their push will take.
    • After stock trading became a major talking point on the campaign trail this fall, Democrats are feeling pressure to push through a bill in the fresh year.
    • But banning trading by members of Congress may not be easy, and some worry the glitch could get bogged down in larger debates over the party’s anti-corruption agenda.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, here at a news conference on Capitol Hill last week, says banning stock trading in Congress is a “high priority.” Now Democrats must decide what form their push will take. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    After stock trading became a major talking point on the campaign trail this fall, Democrats are feeling pressure to push through a bill in the fresh year.

    But banning trading by members of Congress may not be easy, and some worry the glitch could get bogged down in larger debates over the party’s anti-corruption agenda.

    “I’d rather have it be a clean bill focused on stock trading, and not muddy it by adding other topics, even if they’re good policies,” said Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-R.I.

    In a recent development, the incoming majority could plant a flag on government accountability with a broad package ranging from insider trading to campaign finance and more. Or they could zoom in on the stocks glitch with a standalone bill.

    Magaziner said he hasn’t received any assurances from House Democratic leaders, instead describing a “collaborative conversation” about what form the legislation could take.

    “I worry that it would get weighed down under its own weight if you try to load it up with too many things,” Magaziner said, while stressing he would support whatever expected incoming Speaker Hakeem Jeffries decides.

    Meanwhile, more than half of the Democrats in the incoming freshman class are calling for action on Day One of the newly introduced Congress, sending a letter to Jeffries last week suggesting they make a “down payment on much-needed reform” by changing House rules to curb stock trading.

    “Democrats may have won the election, but we have a long way to go to earn back the trust of voters across the country,” reads the letter, led by Reps.-elect Sarah Trone Garriott of Iowa and Jamie Ager of North Carolina. “A stock trading ban alone will not fix Washington, but it is the fastest way to show voters we heard them.”.

    Folding latest language into the House’s internal rules would be a relatively easy path, requiring just a majority vote on the House floor, instead of passage in both chambers and the president’s signature. But such internal limits wouldn’t have the force of law, and some believe it would cool the urgency around the problem while doing little to crack down on insider trading.

    In a recent development, colorado Rep. Jason Crow remarked moving forward rapidly with a rule change wouldn’t preclude passing a bill, suggesting his fellow Democrats do both.

    In a recent development, “I want to pursue a parallel track,” mentioned Crow, who co-chairs the End Corruption Caucus. “We want to move via rule and just prohibit it right out of the gate, or as much as we can.”.

    Jeffries has repeatedly said the topic is high on his to-do list as he looks to deliver on the accountability the “American people are demanding.”.

    Sources indicate that “We’re committed to making sure we pass legislation that bans members of Congress from trading stocks. That will be a high priority,” he stated at a news conference this week.

    But with more than two dozen different bills on the topic introduced over the past few years alone, lawmakers will have to decide exactly what a “ban” means to them.

    Some want to force members of Congress to fully offload their stocks with the exception of widely held mutual funds. Other proposals would block lawmakers from buying new stocks but allow them to keep the ones they already own, like a Republican-led bill that passed the House earlier this year but stalled in the Senate.

    Democrats resisted that push, which was led by outgoing House Administration Chair Bryan Steil, R-Wis., partly because it included an unrelated voter ID provision they called a “poison pill.” Many also complained the measure didn’t go far enough, extending to members’ spouses and dependent children but leaving out key figures in other branches of government, such as the president.

    Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., stated she wants to stay close to the text of a consensus bill she hammered out last year with a small bipartisan group that included Magaziner and Reps. Chip Roy, R-Texas, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa.

    “That is the most comprehensive, thorough, thoughtful proposal and bipartisan proposal that we have,” she remarked of the bill, dubbed the Restore Trust in Congress Act.

    That measure would not apply to President Donald Trump, as many Democrats have urged as they seek to draw attention to his ballooning wealth while in office. Still, Jayapal suggested a presidential stock trading ban could be moved separately.

    In a recent development, “There is discussion about the president, vice president, Cabinet, Supreme Court. I know we’re working on some language around enforcement, around those pieces, but I actually think that can be a separate bill,” Jayapal remarked. “We want to hold everyone accountable — but at minimum, we have to do ourselves.”.

    It has been revealed that it’s not clear how much appetite will exist next year for a bipartisan compromise that could realistically clear a 60-vote cloture threshold in the Senate. Notably, key Republicans who worked on the consensus bill will be leaving Congress, with Roy losing a primary bid for Texas attorney general and Fitzpatrick unseated by a Democratic challenger.

    While lawmakers could in theory advance a latest stock-trading bill even sooner, before Democrats take control of both chambers, time and patience is short in the lame-duck session.

    At a news conference at the Capitol earlier this week with Crow and Jayapal, a group of freshman and returning Democrats took matters into their own hands, promising not to hold or trade individual stocks as part of a broader pledge backed by the Political Integrity Project.

    Industry observers note that “My district, Upcoming York 10, happens to include Wall Street, but I don’t represent Wall Street. I represent the people of Brooklyn and Manhattan who deserve someone who goes to work every single day and demonstrates right up front, ‘I work for you.’ And what better way to prove that than by day one showing we will ban members of Congress from enriching themselves, from trading stocks?” Rep.-elect Brad Lander mentioned.

    While momentum has grown in recent years as key senior lawmakers softened their resistance to a stock trading bill, not everyone is on board. Some members still argue, whether publicly or privately, that they should be able to trade on the stock market just like other citizens or that existing disclosure requirements established by a 2012 law are already enough to discourage dubious trades.

    As they iron out the legislative text of any new bill, members will have to decide how to handle emerging topics such as prediction markets and crypto, along with sticky questions such as whether to allow blind trusts. And extending restrictions to the president could be a nonstarter for many Republicans.

    Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., noted Democrats in the next Congress should look to a bipartisan bill that advanced out of the Senate Homeland and Governmental Affairs Committee in July 2025 as a model.

    “The legislation we passed out of the committee applied to the executive branch,” he mentioned. “But it didn’t take effect for anybody until their next terms, which was a compromise.”.

    It has been revealed that that proposal would apply to future presidents but not the current one, potentially freeing up more Republicans to vote for it without angering Trump. Still, it hasn’t seen action on the Senate floor.

    Hawley said that while he’d like to see a “full ban on trading and holding” in Congress, he would be open to a weaker proposal in the interest of getting something done.

    “I’ll take anything that’s an incremental improvement over what we have now, which is nothing,” he said.

    Aris Folley contributed to this report.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as “The most vital midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.”.

    “When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump noted, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to “blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.”.

    Sources indicate that “If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” Trump stated midway in his speech. “Now that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”.

    The last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the Latest York Times/Siena University polls report “The party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.” The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting “that Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.” If a sweep happens in the toss up races, it’ll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.

    Meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the Latest York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how big a role early votes will play in the outcome.
